Observability: logs, metrics, and traces.
We call “observability” the ability to understand what’s happening in a complex system (in real time if possible).
The fundamental principles of observability are:
•
Curation and participation: Modern observability platforms must enable extreme curation of information. Any information that isn’t curated is prone to being useless and will also consume unnecessary resources (disk, memory…). Participation is a platform feature that allows anyone to easily send information they want to analyze at any time, and ideally, it can be aggregated with information from other sources.
•
Democratization: Not just the system heroes, who have deep knowledge of logs or complex metrics, should understand what’s happening. Observability is truly effective when the entire organization can benefit from the platform and analyze the information to get the results they’re looking for in each business area.
•
Efficiency and Speed: This is more of a highly desirable feature than a principle. But it’s so important that if the observability platform degrades in this regard, the power users will stop using it. It’s necessary to minimize the gap between the appearance of an event (or a specific pattern) and the user’s notification or query. The huge volume of data that needs to be processed makes this feature a real implementation challenge.
Observability in software systems is realized through three main areas: logging, monitoring, and tracing. Although they sometimes overlap, it’s helpful to clarify the scope and main characteristics of each of these techniques. In many cases, the platforms we use to centralize our system’s information can work with all these techniques.

The fundamental characteristic of metrics is that they are aggregable information. They are the logical atoms that enable the generation of counters or histograms over a specific time range, even in real time. Metrics usually don’t have a very broad associated context. They typically indicate what and when something happened in the system, but they don’t provide detailed information on why. For that, we use logging.
Logging, on the other hand, handles discrete events, which are often enriched with context. This context adds very valuable information to the event, allowing us to know in detail what happened and when. Due to the enormous volume and noise they can generate, the logging policy should be tightly controlled.
The definition of tracing revolves around the definition of request. A request is a transaction in our system that has a beginning and end (lifecycle). Tracing is responsible for studying the behavior of requests and their lifecycle. In modern distributed systems, it’s possible to perform tracing by following a request through its processing across different systems; each hop from one system to another is known as a span. This technique is typically used to investigate performance issues and debug specific errors.
